extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of a periodical interested in taste, poetry, manners, and comic essays (readers/contributors to The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_short: writing comic essays and character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing periodical humorous/critical essays and character portraits—covering what makes songs/poems moving, what constitutes a 'fine gentleman', comic treatment of court life, and how to portray absent/distrait characters for humour. Emphasis on moral/ stylistic precepts and vivid illustrative incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural and poetical sentiments / majestick simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Sentiments in that Ballad are extremely natural and poetical, and full of majestick Simplicity” — preference for thoughts and feelings that arise naturally from the subject and present themselves simply and nobly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalness pleases both the common people and refined tastes; it produces the ‘warming of the heart’ and the noble effect admired in ancient poets. Examples quoted: several stanzas of the old ballad compared to passages of the Æneid and Homer. Anti-pattern: overwrought or artificial conceits that obscure simple feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epigrammatical turns and points of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit... it would never have become the Delight of the common People” — caution against replacing natural sentiment with showy epigrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleverness-for-its-own-sake can spoil broad appeal; witty epigrams may please certain readers but lose the universality and heart of a piece. Use restraint if the aim is lasting popular effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sounding language and majestic numbers (meter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Language is ‘majestick, and the Numbers [sonorous]’ — value placed on sonorous diction and noble rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to cadence and sound; ‘sonorous’ lines and appropriate diction ('apparel') can give a poem the ‘majestic’ quality comparable to classics (examples: quoted English stanzas and Latin parallels from Virgil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical simplicity / copying after nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be ‘directed... by the same Kind of Poetical Genius, and by the same Copyings after Nature’ as the ancients — favouring classical simplicity and fidelity to natural feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imitate mannered fashions (the ‘Gothic’ manner); instead, aim for the sort of simplicity and naturalness found in Homer/Virgil. The essay supports claims by juxtaposing English lines with Latin examples to show shared spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify catalogues with little characters
rubrics_metrics.description: In lists (catalogues) of the dead, follow the ancients by ‘diversifying it with little Characters of particular Persons.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing long lists or catalogues, include brief, particularizing details for individuals to humanize the enumeration and produce pathos (example: the Catalogue of the Slain with small character-notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal emotional appeal / warming the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: A good song/poem ‘would... warm the Heart’ and delight people of all ranks; this effect is due to nature in the piece rather than fashionable artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for sentiments and situations that move readers broadly. Examples: the ballad's stanzas that move by their simplicity and natural circumstantial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Gothic manner; prefer restraint and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: “If this Song had been written in the Gothic Manner... it would not have hit the Taste of so many Ages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid transient, perverse affectations and gaudy stylistic tricks that cater to ‘little Wits’; prefer forms and modes that show classical restraint and durable taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine gentleman defined by inner virtues rather than outward dress
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine gentleman’s esteem comes from adherence to ‘the eternal Rules of Reason and good Sense’ and from ‘Humanity and Good-nature’ rather than from elaborate dress or affected airs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying or judging a gentleman, prioritize moral qualities (humanity, virtue, reason) and speech/behaviour over clothes or superficial show. Example critique of ‘Dorimant’ and contrast with 'Ignotus'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unaffected negligence and ease as a mark of breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘By a thorough Contempt of little Excellencies, he is perfectly Master of them... his Negligence is unaffected.’ — true ease should be natural, not studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid studied airs: genuine indifference arises from internal stability (virtue, good fortune, belief) and shows as graceful ease. Portrayal/voice should reflect relaxed composure rooted in character, not performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity, bravery, and philosophical indifference as gentlemanly marks
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To be a Fine Gentleman, is to be a Generous and a Brave Man’ and a belief in a larger order (another life) leads to ‘graceful Unconcern.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize moral courage and generosity as producing good humour and agreeable presence; inner philosophical convictions shape outward carriage and social charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour in a ruler or observer used to correct and test privately
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharamond ‘punished his Courtiers for their Insolence and Folly, not by any Act of Publick Disfavour, but by humorously practising upon their Imaginations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes of private theatrical manipulation or comic experiments to expose vanity and folly—humour as a corrective tool. Examples: Pharamond’s staged notices, altering favour to see effects, setting scenes with Eucrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict how favour or disgrace reshapes self-perception
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Man in Disgrace shall immediately lose all his natural Endowments, and he that finds Favour have the Attributes of an Angel.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satirizing or characterizing social life, show how external status (favour/disgrace) inflates or deflates perceived virtues; this dynamic is a rich source of comic and critical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate thoughtful distraction from mere vacuity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I distinguish a Man who is Absent, because he thinks of something else, from one who is Absent, because he thinks of nothing at all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character sketches and humour, treat distraction as potentially signifying learning, study, or strong passion (mathematicians, lovers), not merely stupidity. This distinction shapes reader sympathy and comic framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for distraction: make learning from surroundings a habit
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Method I took to conquer it was a firm Resolution to learn something from whatever I was obliged to see or hear.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As practical advice (and as a literary device), present characters who cultivate attentiveness by resolving to extract lessons from whatever they observe; use this method as both moral counsel and to construct amusing contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characterization through vivid, absurd particulars (Menalcas examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: La Bruyère’s Menalcas: a catalogue of absurd mishaps (half-shaved, wig caught by candlestick, takes wrong coach, swallows dice, pours wine into the table, sends misaddressed letters, bread multiplying on plate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ specific, concrete, and escalating absurd incidents to create a memorable comic character. These particulars (rather than abstract claims) make the humour vivid and believable; the essay uses numerous such examples to generate amusement and recognition.
